title: East Sikkim in monsoon: planning a June–September trip
meta_description: Visiting Gangtok and East Sikkim from June to September: NH10 landslides and detours, what still works, what to skip, lower prices and what to pack.
summary: Gangtok works in monsoon if you plan for the road. From June to September NH10 along the Teesta is often cut by landslides, so build in a spare day and know the detour via Kalimpong or Pakyong. Gangtok, Rumtek and Ranka stay easy; Tsomgo is often open; North Sikkim and the Silk Route are the riskiest.

sections.heading: What monsoon means in East Sikkim
paras: The south-west monsoon reaches Sikkim in early June and usually retreats by late September. July and August are the wettest months. It rarely rains all day every day; a typical pattern is cloud and drizzle with heavy bursts, often in the afternoon and at night, and the odd clear morning when the hills steam in the sun. Gangtok stays mild, with days in the high teens to low twenties °C, and the forests are at their greenest.

The problem is not the rain in town. It is what the rain does to the mountains. Sikkim's slopes are steep and its rocks are weak schists and phyllites, so saturated hillsides slide. Roads are cut, sometimes for hours and sometimes for weeks. Plan a monsoon trip around the roads, and it can be cheap, quiet and pleasant. Plan it like an October trip, and it can go badly wrong.

sections.heading: NH10 and the detours
paras: NH10 is the main road from Siliguri to Gangtok, about 115–120 km along the Teesta gorge. It is also the road most often broken in monsoon. Several stretches slide year after year, and parts were badly damaged in the Teesta flash flood of October 2023. In 2025 the highway was shut repeatedly, and in July–August 2026 the 20th Mile stretch was closed for weeks.

When NH10 is cut, traffic uses one of two longer routes. The first runs from Siliguri via Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock to Rorathang and on to Gangtok. The second follows NH717A from the plains via Gorubathan and Lava to Rhenock, Rorathang, Pakyong and Ranipool. Either can add 2–4 hours and a few hundred rupees a seat to a shared jeep, or ₹1,000–2,500 to a reserved car, indicative 2026. These roads can slide too.

Before every transfer day, ask your hotel or driver which route is open, and check current status before you travel. The West Bengal and Sikkim police and district administrations post closures, and local drivers know within the hour.

Rail will not solve this yet. The Sivok–Rangpo line, about 45 km, is still under construction and targeted for about 2027, and Pakyong Airport, about 31 km south of Gangtok, has had no scheduled commercial flights in 2026. For now, every traveller reaches Gangtok by road, so the road decides the plan. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A monsoon plan that works
paras: Our usual monsoon trip is simple: three or four nights based in Gangtok, with day trips that can be shuffled. One day in town, one day to Rumtek, Ranka and Lingdum, and one day to Tsomgo and Baba Mandir, with Nathu La added only if the road is open and your permit day works. If the weather closes the high road, you swap days rather than lose them.

Add a spare day at the end. If NH10 is cut on the day you leave, a spare day means a slow drive via Kalimpong instead of a missed flight. Never book a same-day evening flight from Bagdogra or train from NJP on the last day of a monsoon trip; leave at least 6–8 hours of margin, or stay the last night in Siliguri.

Pair Gangtok with Kalimpong or Darjeeling if you have more time. Kalimpong is on one of the detour routes anyway, and its nurseries and markets do well in the rain. Skip long chains such as Gangtok–Zuluk–Aritar or Gangtok–Lachung in July and August; each extra mountain road is another chance of a closure.

sections.heading: June to September, month by month
paras: June starts busy and ends quiet. The first half still has school-holiday crowds from Kolkata and other cities, with the monsoon arriving in the first or second week. Roads are usually still in fair shape early in the month, so June is the best monsoon month for Tsomgo and Nathu La. Prices begin to fall in the second half.

July and August are the heart of the rains. Expect the most NH10 closures, the most cloud at Tsomgo and the lowest hotel rates. These are the months for a slow Gangtok stay with flexible day trips, not for chasing high passes. Leeches are at their worst on forest paths.

September is the turning month. Rain eases through the second half, the hills are still green, and clear mornings become more common. Roads remain fragile after two months of rain, so keep the spare day. By the last week of September, Gangtok starts filling up again ahead of the Durga Puja holidays, and prices climb back towards autumn levels. If you can choose only one monsoon month, we suggest the second half of September.

sections.heading: Prices and crowds
paras: Monsoon is the low season for hotels. After the June school holidays end, many Gangtok hotels cut rates sharply until late September, and walk-in bargaining works. Rooms that cost ₹6,000 in May can often be had for much less. Ask for the off-season rate, and ask whether breakfast is included.

Vehicle prices do not fall as much, because taxi fares in Sikkim are largely fixed. Detours can push them up: a car going via Kalimpong burns more fuel and time, and drivers charge for it. Shared jeep seats may cost a little more on detour days. Agree the price and route before you set off.

The quiet is a real bonus. MG Marg is calm, monasteries are empty in the morning, and the Pang Lhabsol festival at Tsuklakhang usually falls in August or September. Check current status before you travel, since festival dates follow the lunar calendar.

sections.heading: Staying safe on wet mountain roads
paras: Most monsoon trips pass without trouble. These habits keep the odds in your favour.
list: Drive in daylight. Plan transfers to start early and finish by 5 pm.
Do not push a driver to cross a fresh slide. If locals are waiting, wait with them.
Keep the driver's number and your hotel's number saved, since phone signal drops in the Teesta gorge.
Carry water and snacks in the car; a road block can hold you for 2–3 hours.
Avoid walking under steep cuttings during heavy rain, even in Gangtok.
Buy travel insurance that covers trip delay and cancellation, and read the landslide clause.
For North Sikkim, pay only small advances, with a written refund rule if permits are suspended.

sections.heading: What to pack for rain in the hills
paras: Pack light and quick-drying. Cotton jeans stay wet for days in Gangtok's humidity.

A small dry bag for phone and documents is worth more than any gadget on a monsoon trip. Shared jeeps carry bags on the roof under a tarpaulin, so line your bag with a plastic sheet or dry bag too, and keep medicines and chargers in your day bag.
list: A proper rain jacket with a hood, plus a compact umbrella for town.
Shoes with good grip that can get wet, and a spare pair of socks for every day.
Leech socks or long socks to tuck trousers into, for Aritar, Rumtek and forest walks.
A warm fleece for Tsomgo, which is cold and damp at 3,753 m even in July.
Quick-dry trousers and shirts, and one set of dry clothes kept sealed.
Motion-sickness tablets for detour days on winding roads.
A power bank, since power cuts are more common in storms.

faqs.q: Is it safe to visit Gangtok in monsoon
faqs.a: Yes, for most travellers, if you plan for road delays. Gangtok town is safe in the rain, and short trips to Rumtek and Ranka usually run. The risk is on the roads: NH10 and mountain routes can be cut by landslides. Travel in daylight, keep a spare day, follow local advice on closures, and check current status before you travel.

Often, but not reliably. NH10 between Siliguri and Gangtok is frequently cut by landslides in July and August; in 2026 the 20th Mile stretch was closed for weeks in July and August. Traffic then detours via Kalimpong and Rhenock or via Lava and Pakyong, adding 2–4 hours. Ask your hotel the evening before, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Tsomgo Lake in monsoon
faqs.a: Usually yes. The Tsomgo road is often open in June to September, though slides can close it for a day. The lake is frequently in cloud by late morning, so leave Gangtok by 7 am for the best chance of a clear view. Carry a warm layer, as the lake is cold and damp at 3,753 m even in July. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Nathu La open during monsoon
faqs.a: Sometimes. Nathu La is open to Indian tourists on its permitted days, usually Wednesday to Sunday, but landslides on the high road close it more often in monsoon, sometimes after permits are issued. Treat it as a bonus rather than the core of a monsoon trip, and book Tsomgo and Baba Mandir as the main plan. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Should I go to North Sikkim in July or August
faqs.a: We advise against it unless you are flexible. North Sikkim permits for Lachung and Lachen are often suspended after landslides in monsoon; in 2025 they were stopped for weeks after slides in April and June. If you go, pay small advances, get a written refund rule, and keep a Gangtok-based fall-back plan. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are hotels cheaper in Gangtok in monsoon
faqs.a: Yes. After the June school holidays, many Gangtok hotels cut rates sharply until late September, and walk-in bargaining often works. Vehicle fares fall less, because taxi fares are largely fixed and detours cost more fuel. A monsoon trip is usually the cheapest time to stay in a comfortable Gangtok hotel, if you can accept some rain and road delays.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Gangtok in monsoon
faqs.a: A hooded rain jacket, an umbrella, grippy shoes that can get wet, plenty of spare socks, quick-dry clothes, a warm fleece for Tsomgo, leech socks for village and forest walks, a power bank and a dry bag for phone and documents. Line your main bag with plastic, since shared jeeps carry luggage on the roof.

faqs.q: How much buffer time do I need in monsoon
faqs.a: Keep at least one spare day in a Gangtok trip of four nights or more, and never plan a same-day evening flight or train after the drive down. If NH10 is cut, the detour via Kalimpong or Pakyong adds 2–4 hours or more. Many of our monsoon guests stay the last night in Siliguri to remove the risk entirely.

faqs.q: Are there leeches in East Sikkim
faqs.a: Yes, in monsoon, on forest paths and grassy trails at lower and middle altitudes, including around Aritar, Rumtek and Fambong Lho. They are harmless but unpleasant. Wear long socks over your trousers or leech socks, carry salt, check your legs after walks, and stay on paved paths in town. They largely disappear by October.
